pages.title: The Woman Who Touched Jesus' Cloak
also: the woman with the issue of blood
touching the hem of his garment
pages.summary: Jesus is on his way to the house of Jairus, a synagogue leader whose young daughter is dying, and a large crowd presses around him. In that crowd is a woman who has been bleeding for twelve years. She has spent everything on doctors and only grown worse, and her illness has left her weak and shut out from others. She has heard about Jesus and tells herself that if she can only touch his clothes she will be well. She slips up behind him and touches his cloak, and the bleeding stops at once. Jesus feels that power has gone out of him and asks who touched him. His disciples are amazed that he asks, with so many people pushing close, but he keeps looking round. Trembling, the woman comes forward, kneels and tells him everything. He calls her daughter, tells her that her faith has made her well, and sends her away in peace.
pages.look_closer: Notice that Jesus does not let her slip away unseen. A secret healing would have left her afraid and still on the edge of the crowd. By speaking to her in front of everyone, and calling her daughter, he gives her back her place (verses 33-34).
lessons: Desperate people are welcome. She had tried every doctor and had nothing left, and she still came to Jesus (Mark 5:25-28).
Faith can be small and quiet. She said almost nothing and only reached out to touch his cloak, and Jesus called that faith (5:27-28, 34).
Jesus notices one person in a crowd. Many pressed against him, but only one touch was a touch of faith, and he stopped to find her (5:30-32).
He heals more than her body. By calling her daughter and sending her away in peace, he gives her a place among his people again (5:33-34).

context.label: On the way to Jairus' house

passages.label: Twelve years of illness and one touch

pages.title: Jesus Heals the Centurion's Servant
pages.summary: In Capernaum a Roman officer, a centurion in charge of about a hundred soldiers, has a servant he values highly who is sick and close to death. The centurion has heard about Jesus and sends a group of Jewish elders with a request that Jesus come and heal the man. The elders plead for him, saying he deserves this help because he loves their nation and paid for their synagogue. Jesus goes with them, but before he reaches the house the centurion sends friends with a message: he does not feel worthy to have Jesus under his roof, and Jesus only needs to give the word for his servant to be healed. He knows about authority, since his own soldiers obey his orders. Jesus is amazed and tells the crowd that he has not found faith like this even in Israel. When the messengers get back to the house, they find the servant well.
pages.look_closer: Notice who speaks. In Luke the centurion never meets Jesus himself: Jewish elders ask for him, and then friends carry his message. In Matthew's account he speaks to Jesus directly (Matthew 8:5-9).
lessons: Jesus answers need across every boundary. A Roman officer, an outsider to Israel, asks for help, and Jesus goes with the elders at once (Luke 7:3-6).
Humility and faith go together. The centurion thinks himself unworthy of a visit, yet he trusts Jesus completely (7:6-7).
Jesus' word is enough. The healing happens at a distance, with Jesus not even entering the house, just as the centurion expected (7:7-10).
Faith surprises Jesus. He is amazed at a man from outside Israel and holds him up as an example to everyone listening (7:9).

passages.label: The elders plead for a Roman officer

pages.title: Crossing the Jordan River
pages.summary: Early in the morning Joshua and all Israel move from Shittim to the Jordan and camp there before crossing. After three days the officers tell the people that when they see the ark of the covenant carried by the priests, they are to follow it, keeping some distance behind, because they have never traveled this way before. Joshua tells the people to consecrate themselves, for the LORD will do wonders among them tomorrow. Joshua tells them that the living God is among them and will drive out their enemies. The priests carrying the ark are to step into the river, and the moment their feet touch the water, which is at flood stage, the water from upstream stops flowing and piles up in a heap. The people cross on dry ground opposite Jericho, while the priests stand firm in the middle of the riverbed until the whole nation has crossed.
pages.look_closer: The Jordan is at flood stage, yet the water stops when the priests' feet touch it (verse 15). God asks them to step first, then he acts. The priests wait in the middle of the river until everyone has crossed (verse 17).
lessons: Follow where God leads, even on a road you have never traveled (Joshua 3:3-4).
Prepare yourselves. Holiness comes before wonders (Joshua 3:5).
Faith steps into the water before the water stops (Joshua 3:13-15).
God keeps his promise, and his people cross together (Joshua 3:16-17).

pages.title: Deborah the Prophetess and Judge
pages.summary: After Ehud dies, Israel again does evil, and the LORD hands them over to Jabin, king of Canaan, whose commander Sisera has nine hundred iron chariots. After twenty years of harsh oppression the people cry out to the LORD. At that time Deborah, a prophetess, is judging Israel, and people come to her under a palm tree for judgment. She sends for Barak and tells him the LORD commands him to gather ten thousand men at Mount Tabor, and that God will draw Sisera and his chariots to the river Kishon. Barak says he will go only if she goes with him, and she agrees, warning that the honor will go to a woman. When Sisera's army gathers, Deborah says this is the day, and the LORD routs Sisera's whole force. Sisera flees on foot to the tent of Jael, who gives him milk and covers him, and then kills him while he sleeps.
pages.look_closer: The text introduces Deborah without comment: a prophetess, the wife of Lappidoth, judging Israel (verses 4-5). People come to her for judgment, and Barak asks her to go with him. Her leadership is simply part of the story.
lessons: God raises up leaders as he chooses. Deborah judges, prophesies and leads Israel to victory (Judges 4:4-7).
Faith moves first. Deborah tells Barak to go, because the LORD has gone before him (Judges 4:6, 14).
Barak needs Deborah beside him, and she goes, but she warns him that the honor will not be his (Judges 4:8-9).
God can win through unlikely people. Jael, a tent-dweller, ends the fight (Judges 4:17-22).

passages.label: A judge under a palm tree

pages.title: Elijah and the Prophets of Baal on Mount Carmel
also: the contest with the prophets of Baal
pages.summary: After three years without rain, Elijah tells King Ahab to gather all Israel on Mount Carmel, along with Baal's 450 prophets. Elijah asks the people how long they will sit on the fence: if the LORD is the true God, they should follow him, and if Baal is, follow Baal. He proposes a test: each side will prepare a bull on an altar with no fire, and the God who answers by fire is God. The prophets of Baal call from morning until evening, dancing and shouting, and nothing happens, and Elijah mocks them. Then Elijah repairs the LORD's altar with twelve stones, digs a trench, and has the offering and wood soaked with water three times. He prays a short prayer, and fire from the LORD falls and burns up the offering, the wood, the stones and the water. The people fall facedown and cry that the LORD is God. Elijah then prays for rain, and a small cloud grows into a great storm.
pages.look_closer: Elijah's prayer is short, while the prophets of Baal shout for hours (verses 26-29, 36-37). He asks the LORD to answer so that the people will know he is God and that he is turning their hearts back.
lessons: Faith must choose. The people are asked how long they will go back and forth between two opinions (1 Kings 18:21).
False gods are silent, and the LORD answers. Nothing happens for Baal, but fire falls when Elijah prays (1 Kings 18:26-38).
A bold stand rests on a plain prayer: let it be known that you are God, and that you are turning their hearts back (1 Kings 18:36-37).
Elijah keeps praying until the rain comes. He sends his servant to look seven times (1 Kings 18:42-44).

pages.title: Elisha and the Floating Axe Head
pages.summary: The group of prophets who follow Elisha find their meeting place too small, so they ask to go down to the Jordan, cut a log each and build a larger house there. Elisha agrees to go with them. While they are cutting down trees, the iron head of one man's axe flies off its handle and sinks into the water. He cries out to Elisha that the axe was borrowed, which means he now owes its owner for the loss. Elisha asks where it fell, and the man shows him the spot. Elisha cuts a stick and throws it into the water, and the iron rises and floats. "Lift it out," Elisha tells him, and the man reaches out and takes it.
pages.look_closer: The man says the axe was borrowed (verse 5), so he is now in debt to its owner, and Elisha takes his loss seriously. The iron does not float by itself: Elisha throws in a stick (verse 6). The man must still reach out his own hand (verse 7).
lessons: God cares about small, ordinary losses, like a borrowed tool, and not only about great public events (2 Kings 6:5-6).
The man brings his trouble to the prophet at once and shows him exactly where it fell (2 Kings 6:5-6).
What we borrow belongs to someone else, and a loss leaves us in debt. Taking care of it is part of being honest (2 Kings 6:5).
God does what no one else can do: iron does not float, yet he raises it, and the man then takes it himself (2 Kings 6:6-7).

The man could not repay what he had lost, and God cleared his debt. In the same way, our debt of sin was too great for us to pay, and God paid it at the cross, where Jesus died in our place (Colossians 2:13-14).

passages.label: A larger place by the Jordan

pages.title: Esther Saves Her People
also: For such a time as this
pages.summary: Haman has persuaded King Xerxes to order the destruction of all the Jews in the empire. When Mordecai learns of it he tears his clothes and goes into the city in sackcloth, wailing, and the Jews everywhere mourn. Queen Esther, a Jew herself, hears of it and asks what is wrong. Mordecai sends her the decree and begs her to plead with the king. She answers that anyone who goes to the king uninvited can be put to death unless he holds out the gold scepter. Mordecai replies that she will not escape, and asks who knows whether she has been placed in the palace for a time like this. Esther asks the Jews to fast for three days and promises to go in, and if she perishes, she perishes. The king holds out the scepter, and at two banquets she names Haman as the enemy. The king has him hanged on the gallows he built for Mordecai.
pages.look_closer: God is not named in the book of Esther, yet the story is full of timing: a queen in the right place, a king who cannot sleep (6:1), a plot turned back on its maker. Mordecai's question, 'Who knows?', is the heart of it (4:14).
lessons: Position is for a purpose. Mordecai tells Esther that her place in the palace may be for such a time as this (Esther 4:14).
Courage is costly and prepared. Esther asks for fasting before she steps in, and then she goes (Esther 4:15-16).
She is brave and wise. She does not rush, but prepares two banquets before she names the danger (Esther 5:4-8; 7:3-6).
Evil plans can fall on those who make them. Haman is hanged on his own gallows (Esther 7:9-10).

pages.title: Ezra Reads the Law to the People
also: Ezra and the Book of the Law
pages.summary: When the seventh month comes, all the people gather at the square by the Water Gate and ask Ezra the scribe to fetch the Book of the Law of Moses. Ezra reads it aloud from daybreak until noon to the men, the women and everyone old enough to understand. He stands on a high wooden platform, and when he opens the book all the people stand. He praises the LORD, and they answer Amen, Amen, lift their hands and bow down. The Levites help the people understand by explaining the reading. When the people begin to weep at the words, Nehemiah, Ezra and the Levites tell them this is a holy day: they should eat, drink, share with those who have nothing, and not be sad, because the LORD's own joy is their strength. The next day the leaders study the Law further and find the command about living in booths. The people build them and celebrate for seven days with great joy.
pages.look_closer: The reading is not enough on its own: the Levites explain it so the people can understand (verses 7-8). Understanding brings first tears, and then joy (verses 9-12). The next day they keep reading and find something to do: build booths (verses 13-15).
lessons: God's people hunger for his word. They ask Ezra to bring out the Book (Nehemiah 8:1).
Reading must lead to understanding. The Levites explain it so that everyone can follow (Nehemiah 8:7-8).
Joy, not only sorrow, belongs with God's word. The joy of the LORD becomes their strength (Nehemiah 8:9-12).
Hearing becomes doing. They find the command about booths and obey it at once (Nehemiah 8:14-17).

passages.label: The Book of the Law is read

pages.title: Gideon and His 300 Soldiers
pages.summary: Gideon and his army camp by the spring of Harod, with the Midianites in the valley to the north. The LORD tells Gideon he has too many men, because Israel might boast that it saved itself, so anyone afraid may go home, and twenty-two thousand leave. At the water the LORD sorts the ten thousand who remain, and only three hundred are chosen. That night, afraid, Gideon goes with his servant to the enemy camp and overhears a man tell a dream about a loaf of barley bread tumbling into the camp, and another says it is the sword of Gideon. Gideon worships and returns to wake his men. He divides them into three companies, each with a trumpet and a jar with a torch inside. At his signal they blow the trumpets, smash the jars, hold up the torches and shout their battle cry in honor of the LORD and Gideon. The Midianites are thrown into panic, turn on one another and flee.
pages.look_closer: God cuts the army from thirty-two thousand to three hundred so that Israel cannot say it saved itself (verses 2-7). Gideon is still afraid, and God gives him a way to hear encouragement (verses 10-15). The weapons are trumpets, jars and torches (verse 16).
lessons: God does not need big numbers. He wants it to be clear that the victory is his (Judges 7:2).
He meets fearful servants where they are, and gives Gideon courage through the enemy's own dream (Judges 7:10-15).
Unusual weapons and plain obedience are enough. Trumpets, jars and torches do the work (Judges 7:16-20).
Give God the credit. Their battle cry names the LORD first, and then Gideon (Judges 7:18, 20).

passages.label: A dream in the enemy camp

pages.title: Isaiah's Vision in the Temple
pages.summary: In the year King Uzziah dies, Isaiah sees the Lord sitting on a high throne, and the hem of his robe fills the temple. Seraphim with six wings stand above him, calling to one another that the LORD of Armies is holy, holy, holy, and that his glory fills the whole earth. The doorposts shake and the temple fills with smoke. Isaiah cries out that he is ruined, because he is a man of unclean lips living among a people of unclean lips, and his eyes have seen the King. One of the seraphim flies to him with a burning coal taken from the altar, touches it to his mouth, and says that his guilt is taken away and his sin atoned for. Then Isaiah hears the Lord asking whom he can send, and he answers: Here am I; send me. The Lord gives him a hard message for a people who will hear but not understand, and promises that a holy seed will remain.
pages.look_closer: Isaiah's first words are not 'Here am I' but 'Woe to me' (verse 5). He sees God's holiness, then his own sin, then is cleansed (verses 3-7), and only then does he hear the call and answer (verse 8). The mission begins with cleansing.
lessons: A true sight of God shows us our need. Isaiah sees the holy King and cries out about his sin (Isaiah 6:1-5).
God himself deals with sin. The burning coal touches Isaiah's mouth, and his guilt is taken away (Isaiah 6:6-7).
A cleansed person is ready to be sent. Isaiah offers himself when the Lord asks who will go (Isaiah 6:8).
God's message may be hard and the work long, but a remnant remains (Isaiah 6:9-13).

passages.label: Unclean lips and a burning coal

pages.title: Jacob Wrestles with God
pages.summary: On his way home to meet his brother Esau, whom he cheated years before, Jacob sends his family and everything he owns across the stream and stays behind alone. A man wrestles with him until daybreak. When the man sees that he cannot overpower Jacob, he touches the socket of Jacob's hip, and it is wrenched. The man says to let him go because day is breaking, but Jacob says he will not let go unless the man blesses him. The man asks his name, and when Jacob answers, he says he will be called Israel instead of Jacob, because he has struggled with God and with people and has won. Jacob asks for his name, but the man only blesses him. Jacob names the place Peniel, saying he has seen God face to face and yet his life was spared. The sun rises as he crosses, limping because of his hip.
pages.look_closer: Jacob wins the struggle but leaves limping (verses 25, 31). The man gives him a new name: Israel, which means 'he struggles with God' (verse 28). What Jacob wanted was not victory but a blessing (verse 26).
lessons: God meets us in the night before the meeting we fear. Jacob is about to face Esau, and first he faces God (Genesis 32:22-24).
Hold on to God until he blesses. Jacob will not let go (Genesis 32:26).
God changes names and people. Jacob the grabber becomes Israel (Genesis 32:27-28).
A blessing can leave a mark. Jacob walks away limping, and he is different from then on (Genesis 32:25, 31).

pages.title: Jesus Heals a Man Born Blind
also: the blind man healed with mud
I was blind, but now I see
pages.summary: Jesus sees a man who has been blind from birth. His disciples ask whose sin caused it, and Jesus answers that it was no one's sin: God's works are to be shown in him. Jesus makes mud with spit, puts it on the man's eyes and tells him to wash in the Pool of Siloam. The man goes, washes and comes back able to see. His neighbors can hardly believe it, and because it is a Sabbath he is brought to the Pharisees, who are divided about Jesus. They question his parents, who are afraid and tell them to ask their son. The man answers that he knows one thing: he was blind and now he sees. When he argues that Jesus must be from God, they throw him out. Jesus finds him, and the man says he believes and worships him.
pages.look_closer: Follow the man's growing confession. First he knows only 'the man they call Jesus' (verse 11), then 'a prophet' (verse 17), then he argues that Jesus must be from God (verse 33), and finally he worships him (verse 38).
lessons: Jesus does not blame the man or his parents. Suffering is not always a punishment, and God can show his works through it (John 9:2-3).
Sight comes with obedience: the man goes and washes as he is told (John 9:7).
A simple testimony is hard to argue with: I was blind, and now I see. Telling what Jesus has done does not need a speech (John 9:25).
Those who could see everything were the ones who refused to see Jesus. Spiritual blindness is turning away from the light (John 9:39-41).
Jesus finds the man after he is thrown out. Those who stand up for him are not left alone (John 9:34-35).

pages.title: Jesus Heals a Paralytic
also: the paralyzed man lowered through the roof
the four friends and the roof
pages.summary: Jesus is back in Capernaum, and so many people gather at the house where he is teaching that there is no room left, not even at the door. Four men bring a paralyzed friend on a mat, but they cannot get through the crowd. So they climb up, make an opening in the roof above Jesus and lower the man down on his mat. Seeing their faith, Jesus tells the man his sins are forgiven. Some teachers of the law think to themselves that only God can forgive sins. Jesus knows what they are thinking and asks which is easier: telling the man his sins are forgiven, or telling him to rise and walk. To prove that the Son of Man has the right to forgive sins here on earth, he tells the man to stand, take his mat and go home. The man does so at once, and everyone is amazed and praises God.
pages.look_closer: Jesus answers the unspoken question before he heals. The friends came for a cure, and the first thing he says is about forgiveness (verse 5). Then the healing becomes the proof of his right to forgive (verses 10-11).
lessons: Determined friends can carry someone to Jesus. These four will not let a crowd or a roof stop them (Mark 2:3-4).
Jesus sees their faith, and the first thing he says is that the man's sins are forgiven. The deepest need is not always the one we bring (Mark 2:5).
Only God can forgive sins, as the teachers say. Jesus' words and his healing show that he has that authority (Mark 2:7, 10-12).
The result is praise. The crowd glorifies God and says they have never seen anything like it (Mark 2:12).

pages.title: Jesus Prays in Gethsemane
pages.summary: After the supper Jesus goes with his disciples to Gethsemane and tells them to sit while he prays. He takes Peter, James and John with him and begins to be deeply troubled. He tells them he is overwhelmed with sorrow to the point of death and asks them to stay and keep watch with him. Going a little further, he falls with his face to the ground and prays that, if it is possible, this cup may pass from him, yet not his own will but the Father's be done. He comes back and finds the three asleep. He warns Peter to watch and pray so they do not give in to temptation, since the spirit is eager but the body is weak. He prays the same prayer a second and a third time, and each time finds them sleeping. Then he says the hour is near: the Son of Man is being betrayed, and his betrayer is close.
pages.look_closer: Jesus asks his three closest friends to stay awake with him, and they fall asleep three times (verses 38-45). His prayer never changes in its heart: if it is possible, let the cup pass, but not what he wants, what the Father wants (verses 39, 42).
lessons: Jesus is honest about his sorrow. He does not hide that he is distressed, and he takes it to his Father in prayer (Matthew 26:37-39).
His prayer ends in surrender: not my will, but yours. Real prayer can ask for another way and still say yes to God's will (Matthew 26:39, 42).
Even good friends grow tired. The disciples want to stay awake but cannot, and Jesus tells them to watch and pray against temptation (Matthew 26:40-41).
He does not run from what is coming. He gets up and goes to meet it (Matthew 26:45-46).

passages.label: Sleeping disciples, and 'your will be done'

pages.title: Martha and Mary
also: Mary has chosen the better part
pages.summary: As Jesus and his disciples travel, he comes to a village where a woman named Martha welcomes him into her home. Her sister Mary sits at the Lord's feet, listening to what he says. Martha, meanwhile, is distracted by all the preparations and finally comes to Jesus and asks whether he does not care that her sister has left her to do the serving alone. She tells him to tell Mary to help her. The Lord answers gently, saying her name twice. She is worried and troubled about many things, he says, but only one thing is needed. Mary has chosen what is better, and no one will take it from her.
pages.look_closer: Jesus does not tell Martha that serving is wrong. He names what is happening inside her: she is worried and bothered (verse 41). The things on her list are many; what Mary chose is one (verse 42).
lessons: Welcoming Jesus can mean hard work, and that is a good thing. Martha opens her home to him (Luke 10:38).
Listening comes first. Mary sits at his feet and takes in his words (Luke 10:39).
Busyness can crowd out the one thing that matters. Jesus gently shows Martha what she is missing (Luke 10:40-42).
Jesus defends the listener. What Mary chose will not be taken from her (Luke 10:42).

pages.title: Mary Anoints Jesus
pages.summary: Six days before the Passover, Jesus comes to Bethany, where Lazarus lives, the man he raised from the dead. A dinner is given in his honor: Martha serves, and Lazarus sits at the table with Jesus. Mary takes a pint of very costly perfume made of pure nard, pours it on Jesus' feet and wipes them with her hair, and the whole house fills with the scent. Judas Iscariot, who will betray Jesus, objects that the perfume could have been sold for three hundred denarii, with the proceeds going to the poor. John explains that Judas does not care about the poor; he is a thief who helps himself to the money bag. Jesus tells him to leave Mary alone. She has kept the perfume for the day of his burial, and he will not always be with them.
pages.look_closer: Compare the two reactions in the room. Mary acts without saying a word; Judas speaks about the poor, and John tells us his real reason (verses 3-6). Jesus says what her act means: it points to his burial (verse 7).
lessons: Costly love for Jesus is never wasted. Mary gives something worth about a year's wages, and Jesus speaks up for her (John 12:3, 5, 7).
Fine words can hide a wrong heart. Judas sounds generous, but John says he was stealing from the money bag (John 12:4-6).
Jesus is not dismissing the poor; elsewhere he commands care for them. He is saying that this time with him will not come again (John 12:8).
Jesus links her gift to his burial, a quiet reminder of where the week is heading (John 12:7).

pages.title: Paul's Conversion on the Damascus Road
also: Saul on the road to Damascus
the light on the Damascus road
pages.summary: Saul, later known as Paul, is still breathing threats against the Lord's followers. He asks the high priest for letters of introduction to the Damascus synagogues, which will let him arrest any men or women of the Way and bring them to Jerusalem. Near Damascus a light from heaven flashes around him and he falls to the ground. A voice asks why he is persecuting him, and when Saul asks who is speaking, the answer is Jesus. Saul is told to go into the city and wait. He cannot see, and for three days he neither eats nor drinks. The Lord sends Ananias to him, though Ananias is afraid of Saul. Ananias lays his hands on him and says Jesus has sent him so that Saul can regain his sight and receive the fullness of the Holy Spirit. Something like scales falls from Saul's eyes, and he is baptized. At once he begins to tell people in the synagogues that Jesus is the Son of God.
pages.look_closer: Notice how personal Jesus is: he asks why Saul is persecuting him, not his followers (verse 4). Hurting his people is hurting him. Notice also Ananias, who argues with the Lord and yet goes (verses 13-17). Obedience is the key.
lessons: Jesus is so close to his people that harming them is harming him (Acts 9:4-5).
No one is too far gone. The man who hunted the church becomes one of its most important messengers (Acts 9:1-2, 15).
God works through ordinary believers like Ananias. He is afraid, but he goes and calls Saul his brother (Acts 9:10-17).
The change shows in what Saul does next: he is baptized, eats, and begins at once to speak about Jesus (Acts 9:18-20).
pages.doctrine_note: Christians understand baptism and being filled with the Holy Spirit in different ways, including how the two relate and whether they come together or at different times. This page says only what the text says.

pages.title: Peter and Cornelius
pages.summary: In Caesarea lives Cornelius, a Roman centurion who is devout and gives generously. One afternoon an angel tells him God has noticed his prayers and gifts, and that he must send for a man named Simon Peter in Joppa. The next day, on a rooftop, Peter sees a large sheet full of animals and hears a voice tell him to kill and eat. He refuses, and the voice answers that what God has made clean, Peter must not treat as unclean. This happens three times. As Peter wonders what it means, the Spirit tells him three men are looking for him and he should go with them. At Cornelius' house Peter says God has shown him to call no one unclean, and he tells the gathering about Jesus. While he is still speaking, the Holy Spirit falls on everyone who hears, and they speak in tongues and praise God. Peter orders them to be baptized.
pages.look_closer: Peter's vision is about food, but its meaning is about people (verses 15, 28). Notice the order: God moves first in Cornelius, then in Peter, then in the whole gathering, and Peter says he now truly understands that God does not show favoritism (verses 34-35).
lessons: God hears the prayers of those outside the usual circle. Cornelius' prayers and gifts rise before him (Acts 10:2, 4).
God changes Peter's heart before he changes his road. Peter must learn to call no one unclean (Acts 10:15, 28).
The good news is for every nation. Everyone who believes in Jesus receives forgiveness of sins (Acts 10:34-35, 43).
The Holy Spirit is poured out on the Gentiles as on the first believers, and the Jewish believers with Peter are astonished (Acts 10:44-47).
pages.doctrine_note: Christians understand how people receive the Holy Spirit, speaking in tongues, and the place of baptism in different ways, including their order. This page says only what the text says: the Spirit came while Peter was speaking, they spoke in tongues, and then they were baptized.

pages.title: Peter Denies Jesus
pages.summary: At the table Jesus tells Simon Peter that Satan has asked to sift the disciples like wheat, but that he has prayed for Peter so his faith will not fail, and that once Peter has turned back he must strengthen the others. Peter insists he is ready to go to prison and even to die with Jesus. Jesus answers that before the rooster crows that day Peter will say three times that he does not know him. Later, after Jesus is arrested, Peter follows at a distance into the high priest's courtyard and sits by the fire. A servant girl, then another person, then a third man says he was with Jesus, and each time Peter denies it. As he speaks the third time, a rooster crows, and Jesus turns and looks at him. Peter remembers the warning, goes outside and weeps bitterly.
pages.look_closer: Notice that the warning comes with a promise: Jesus has prayed for Peter, and Peter will turn back (verse 32). In the courtyard the text does not say what the look meant; it tells only what Peter remembered and what he did next (verses 61-62).
lessons: Strong promises are not the same as strength. Peter means every word he says, and still fails within hours (Luke 22:33, 54-62).
Failure is not the end of the story. Jesus prayed for Peter's faith before he failed, and gave him a task for afterwards (Luke 22:31-32).
Fear can make a bold person quiet. Peter follows at a distance, and the denials come one after another (Luke 22:54-60).
Real sorrow is the first step back. Peter's tears show he knows what he has done, and the story of his return is told in John's Gospel (Luke 22:61-62; John 21:15-17).

pages.title: Peter Freed from Prison
pages.summary: King Herod has James, the brother of John, killed with the sword, and arrests Peter during the Feast of Unleavened Bread, putting him in prison under sixteen soldiers. The church prays earnestly for him. The night before his trial, Peter sleeps between two soldiers, bound with chains, with guards at the door. Suddenly an angel appears and a light shines in the cell. He strikes Peter's side, tells him to get up, and the chains fall off. The angel tells him to dress and follow him. They pass the guards and the iron gate to the city, which opens by itself, and the angel leaves him. Peter goes to the house of Mary, mother of John Mark, where many are praying. A servant girl, Rhoda, recognizes his voice and is so happy that she runs to tell them without opening the door, and they tell her she is out of her mind. Peter keeps knocking, and when they open the door, they are astonished.
pages.look_closer: The church is praying for Peter, and when he arrives they do not believe it is him (verses 5, 12-16). Luke is honest about how surprised people can be by answered prayer. James dies and Peter lives, with no explanation (verses 2, 11).
lessons: The church prays, and God acts. They pray earnestly while Peter is in prison (Acts 12:5).
God's rescue can be quiet and unexpected. An angel, a light and a gate that opens by itself (Acts 12:7-10).
Answered prayer can surprise even those who prayed (Acts 12:13-16).
God does not always rescue in the same way. James dies, and Peter is freed (Acts 12:2, 11).

pages.title: Stephen, the First Martyr
pages.summary: Stephen, a man of great faith, filled with the Holy Spirit, does wonders among the people. Men from several synagogues argue with him but cannot answer the wisdom the Spirit gives him, so they stir up the people and bring him before the council. The council members see that his face looks like the face of an angel. In his long reply Stephen retells Israel's history, then says his hearers are stubborn people who always resist the Holy Spirit, as their ancestors did. They are furious, but Stephen, full of the Holy Spirit, looks up and sees God's glory, with Jesus standing at his right hand. They cover their ears, rush at him, drag him out of the city and stone him, with a young man named Saul watching over their coats. As he dies, Stephen prays that the Lord Jesus will receive his spirit, and that the Lord will not hold this sin against them.
pages.look_closer: Stephen's last words echo Jesus' words on the cross: he commits his spirit to the Lord and asks forgiveness for those killing him (7:59-60; Luke 23:34, 46). And the one watching the coats is Saul (7:58).
lessons: A Spirit-filled life shows in character and courage. Stephen is full of faith, grace and the Holy Spirit (Acts 6:8-10).
Truth spoken plainly can still be rejected. The council is furious (Acts 7:51-54).
Jesus stands to receive his servant. Stephen sees heaven open (Acts 7:55-56).
Forgiveness has the last word. Stephen asks God not to hold the sin against them (Acts 7:59-60).

pages.title: The Ascension of Jesus
pages.summary: Luke opens the book of Acts by looking back at everything Jesus began to do and to teach, right up to the day he was lifted into heaven. After his suffering, Jesus shows himself alive to the apostles with many convincing proofs over forty days, speaking about the kingdom of God. He tells them not to leave Jerusalem but to wait for the gift the Father promised: in a few days they will be baptized with the Holy Spirit. The apostles ask whether he will now restore the kingdom to Israel. Jesus says the times belong to the Father, but they will receive power when the Spirit comes and will be his witnesses from Jerusalem to the ends of the earth. Then he is lifted up as they watch, and a cloud hides him. Two men in white tell them that this same Jesus will return.
pages.look_closer: The apostles ask about the kingdom and Israel, and Jesus does not give them a date. He gives them something to do instead: wait, receive power and be witnesses (verses 6-8). The two men ask why they keep looking at the sky, and promise that he will come back (verses 10-11).
lessons: Jesus does not leave his friends with an empty promise. He rises, shows himself alive, and prepares them for what comes next (Acts 1:3-5).
The power to be a witness comes from the Holy Spirit, not from the apostles' own strength (Acts 1:8).
His work reaches outward in steps: Jerusalem, Judea, Samaria, and the ends of the earth. The task is bigger than any one place (Acts 1:8).
He goes up, and he is coming back. Believers live between the two, waiting and working (Acts 1:9-11).
pages.doctrine_note: Christians understand the promised baptism with the Holy Spirit, and the return of Jesus, in different ways, including when and how each happens and how they are shown. This page says only what the text says.

pages.title: The Birth of Isaac
also: Hagar and Ishmael in the wilderness
pages.summary: The LORD does for Sarah what he promised: at exactly the time God had said, she becomes pregnant and bears Abraham a son in his old age. Abraham names him Isaac and circumcises him on the eighth day, as God commanded. Abraham is a hundred years old, and Sarah says that God has made her laugh and that everyone who hears will laugh with her. When Isaac is weaned, Abraham gives a great feast. Sarah sees Ishmael, Hagar's son, mocking, and tells Abraham to send Hagar and her son away. This troubles Abraham, but God tells him to listen to Sarah, for Isaac is the child of promise, and promises to make a nation of Ishmael too. Abraham sends Hagar off with bread and water. In the wilderness, when the water is gone, God hears the boy's cry and opens Hagar's eyes to a well, and Ishmael grows up.
pages.look_closer: The name Isaac means 'he laughs'. Abraham laughed when he was told of this son (Genesis 17:17), Sarah laughed (18:12), and now she says God has given her laughter (21:6). God also hears Ishmael, not only Isaac (21:17).
lessons: God keeps his promises in his own time, even when it seems impossible (Genesis 21:1-2).
Laughter can change. It begins as doubting laughter and becomes joyful laughter (Genesis 17:17; 18:12; 21:6).
God hears the cry of those who are sent away. He cares for Hagar and Ishmael (Genesis 21:17-19).
The promise comes through Isaac, but God's care is wider than the line of promise (Genesis 21:12-13).

pages.title: The Miraculous Catch of Fish
pages.summary: One day, with the crowd pressing around him to hear God's word, Jesus stands by the Lake of Gennesaret and sees two empty boats, their owners washing their nets. He gets into Simon's boat, asks him to push out a little, and teaches the people from the boat. When he finishes, he tells Simon to go into deep water and let down the nets. Simon answers that they have worked all night and caught nothing, but because Jesus says so, he will do it. They catch so many fish that the nets begin to break, and they signal their partners in the other boat, and both boats begin to sink. Simon Peter falls at Jesus' knees and says he is a sinful man and Jesus should go away. Jesus tells him not to be afraid: from now on he will catch people. They bring their boats to shore, leave everything and follow him.
pages.look_closer: Peter calls Jesus Master (verse 5) and obeys against his own experience. After the catch he calls him Lord (verse 8). He says 'Go away from me', but Jesus says 'Do not be afraid' and gives him new work (verses 8-10).
lessons: Obey even when your experience says it will not work. Simon lets down the nets because Jesus says so (Luke 5:5).
Seeing Jesus' power shows us who we are. Peter sees his own sinfulness (Luke 5:8).
Jesus answers fear with a call: do not be afraid, from now on you will catch people (Luke 5:10).
Following Jesus means leaving something behind. They leave everything and follow him (Luke 5:11).

pages.title: The Sermon on the Mount
pages.summary: Seeing the crowds, Jesus goes up on a mountainside, sits down, and his disciples come to him. He begins with blessings on the poor in spirit, those who mourn, the gentle, those who hunger for what is right, the merciful, the pure in heart, the peacemakers and the persecuted, promising them the kingdom, comfort, mercy and the sight of God. He tells his followers they are the salt of the earth and the light of the world, and that their good deeds should lead others to praise the Father. He teaches them to pray in private, without empty repeating, and gives a model prayer that begins with Our Father in heaven. He tells them not to worry about food or clothes, for the Father who feeds the birds and clothes the lilies cares for them, and to seek his kingdom first. He ends with two builders, one on rock and one on sand, and the crowds are amazed because he teaches with authority.
pages.look_closer: Jesus starts with who is blessed before he says what to do (5:3-12). The teaching moves from the heart to the deed: prayer, money, worry, and finally doing what he says (7:24-27). The crowd's wonder is about his authority (7:28-29).
lessons: God's kingdom values are different from the world's. Blessing is for the poor in spirit and the gentle (Matthew 5:3-10).
Believers are meant to be seen. Salt and light show God's goodness in daily life (Matthew 5:13-16).
Prayer is simple and personal, spoken to our Father who knows what we need (Matthew 6:5-13).
Seek God's kingdom first, and do not be consumed by worry (Matthew 6:25-34).
Hearing is not enough. Building on Jesus' words means doing them (Matthew 7:24-27).

pages.title: The Transfiguration
pages.summary: Six days later Jesus takes Peter, James and John to the top of a high mountain, away from everyone else. There he is changed before their eyes: his face shines like the sun and his clothes become as white as light. Moses and Elijah appear and talk with him. Peter says it is good to be there and offers to put up three shelters, one for each of them. While he is still speaking, a bright cloud covers them and a voice from the cloud says that this is God's beloved Son, with whom he is well pleased, and that they must listen to him. The disciples fall on their faces in fear, but Jesus touches them and tells them to get up and not be afraid. When they look up they see only Jesus. As they come down, he tells them to keep the vision secret until the Son of Man rises from the dead.
pages.look_closer: Moses, who gave the Law, and Elijah, a great prophet, stand with Jesus, yet the voice says to listen to him, and when the cloud lifts only Jesus remains (verses 3, 5, 8).
lessons: Jesus' glory is real. For a moment the three disciples see him as he truly is (Matthew 17:2).
The Father speaks: listen to him. Everything Moses and the prophets taught leads to Jesus (Matthew 17:5; Luke 24:27).
Peter wants to stay on the mountain, but the work is down below. Mountaintop moments prepare us for ordinary days (Matthew 17:4, 9).
Do not be afraid. Jesus' touch and his words meet the disciples' fear (Matthew 17:6-7).

pages.title: The Triumphal Entry
also: Hosanna to the Son of David
pages.summary: As Jesus and his disciples come near Jerusalem, at Bethphage on the Mount of Olives, he sends two of them ahead into the village. They will find a donkey tied up with her colt beside her, and they are to untie them and bring them to him, saying that the Lord needs them. Matthew explains that this fulfills the prophet's words about a gentle king riding on a donkey. The disciples do as Jesus said, lay their cloaks on the animals, and Jesus rides. A huge crowd spreads cloaks on the road, and others cut branches from trees and lay them down as well. The crowds in front and behind shout Hosanna to the Son of David and bless the one who comes in the Lord's name. The whole city is stirred and asks who this is, and the crowds answer that he is the prophet Jesus from Nazareth in Galilee.
pages.look_closer: Matthew points back to the prophet Zechariah: the king comes gentle, on a donkey, not on a warhorse (verses 4-5). The crowd shouts about the Son of David, yet the city asks who he is, and the answer is only 'the prophet from Nazareth' (verses 9-11).
lessons: Jesus comes as a gentle king, on a donkey, not with armies. His kingdom looks different from the kingdoms of this world (Matthew 21:4-5).
The disciples trust Jesus' instructions even when they sound strange, and everything happens just as he said (Matthew 21:2-3, 6).
The crowd welcomes him with cloaks, branches and shouts of Hosanna. Praise is the right welcome for the King who comes (Matthew 21:8-9).
Many shout Hosanna, but the city still asks who he is. Welcoming Jesus means knowing who he really is (Matthew 21:10-11).

passages.label: Hosanna to the Son of David

pages.title: The Woman Caught in Adultery
also: he who is without sin cast the first stone
pages.summary: Early in the morning Jesus is teaching in the temple courts when the scribes and Pharisees bring a woman caught in adultery and make her stand in front of the crowd. They remind him that the law of Moses says such a woman should be stoned, and ask what he says, hoping to trap him. Jesus bends down and writes in the dirt with his finger. When they keep asking, he stands up and says that the one who has no sin should throw the first stone, and he stoops down and writes again. Hearing this, they leave one by one, the older ones first, until Jesus is left alone with the woman. He asks her where they are and whether no one has condemned her. She says no one, Lord. Jesus says he does not condemn her either, and tells her to go and leave her life of sin.
pages.look_closer: Notice the order in Jesus' last words: first mercy, then the call to leave sin (verse 11). The accusers use the woman as a test for Jesus (verse 6), and he turns the test back on their own hearts (verse 7). What he wrote on the ground is not told.
lessons: Jesus will not be trapped. His answer takes the law seriously and still shows mercy (John 8:6-7).
Honest hearts have no stones to throw. Everyone has sinned (John 8:7-9).
Mercy comes before the call to change. He does not condemn her, and then he tells her to leave her life of sin (John 8:10-11).
Jesus is the only one without sin who could have thrown the first stone, and he chooses to forgive (John 8:7, 11).

passages.label: Go, and leave your life of sin

pages.doctrine_note: Some early Greek manuscripts do not contain this passage, and Bibles treat it in different ways. This page tells it as it stands in the Bible text used here.

pages.title: Water into Wine at Cana
pages.summary: On the third day there is a wedding at Cana in Galilee. Jesus' mother is there, and Jesus and his disciples are invited too. When the wine runs out, Mary tells Jesus, and although he says his hour has not yet come, she tells the servants to do whatever he asks. Six large stone water jars stand nearby, kept for Jewish washing ceremonies. Jesus tells the servants to fill them with water, and they fill them to the brim. He then tells them to scoop some out and bring it to the master of the banquet, who tastes it and finds that it has become wine. He calls the bridegroom and says most hosts serve the best wine first, but this one has kept the best until now. This is the first of Jesus' signs, and his disciples believe in him.
pages.look_closer: Only the servants and the disciples know where the wine came from (verses 9 and 11). The master of the banquet simply notices how good it is. John says the sign showed Jesus' glory and led his disciples to believe.
lessons: Jesus cares about ordinary needs, even the embarrassment of a wedding that has run out of wine (John 2:3-5).
Mary points the servants to Jesus with simple advice: do whatever he tells you. Obedience comes before the miracle (John 2:5-8).
The best is not always served first. Jesus gives the finest wine last, and he gives more than anyone expects (John 2:9-10).
A sign points beyond itself. It shows Jesus' glory, and his disciples put their faith in him (John 2:11).
